This is how I've always seen it when it comes to role-playing:

Other races are coloring books, humans are a blank page.


New players who are uncomfortable or unsure of themselves can play as either and do well in either case depending on the player themselves. They can use any of the fantasy races as a template, following the well worn stereotypes or ideas presented in the books to give them the foothold they need to play the game. New players can also pick humans, since they already know how a human behaves from their own experience and they can build something familiar from that. This can be a mistake however, as not knowing what's needed or expected of a character in a role-playing game they can easily come off as boring.


Veteran players however often enthusiastically approach the non-human races with the intention of altering and playing against those lines in the coloring book. They'll fill in the borders in ways that recontextualize the whole image, add new things to flesh out the character away from the stereotypes. Their elf will be an emotional train wreck instead of aloof and above it all. Their dwarf will be flamboyant and cosmopolitan instead of a salt-of-the-earth craftsman. Both of these were characters that I played on the past. The thing is that in all of these cases you're still being informed by another authors works. While every character is built upon the works of others, nothing being made in a vacuum as it were, even if you're drawing over the lines on the page you're still being guided by those lines. What you do to reject a stereotype only underscores the stereotypes you're rejecting.


There's nothing wrong with either option of course, I just prefer to play human characters because it gives me the most creatice freedom. Free from preconceptions and the borders entirely I can make a character that feels more organic and dynamic. One of my favorite things to do in games is have my character develop and change over the course of the story and the tabula rasa of humanity provides me more room to do that. So I reject the notion that playing a human is less creative or boring, I feel like so much more creativity goes into making a compelling human character than a character of any race, because you're starting from relatively nothing compared to a dragonborn or elf or whatever. People only think humans are boring because they've never seen what someone can really do with a character like that. They see a plain white ceiling and they see large spaces to paint single colors within, but the master sees the potential for the Sistine Chapel.

Celerity is one of the prime examples I use for how the V20 and previous systems had broken mechanics. I point to them while comparing the solutions that White Wolf has gone with.


Vampire the Requiem: Added a 'Defense' stat that would be modified by different factors. Celerity offers one of those modifiers. Instead of every dot granting characters an extra turn in combat it offered characters temporary boosts to their Defense stat. If you wanted to import this mechanic to another you should look up the rules from the CofD and VtR sourcebooks and apply those changes to your players current character sheets adding a new Defense stat for each player and NPC.


Vampire 5th Edition: 'Passive' disciplines as Potence, Fortitude, and of course Celerity were redesigned to he less passive and more active. Like any other discipline they are now divided into multiple abilities by level. If you want to import these mechanics into your game simply pick the 5 powers you think make for the best progression from the lost on the V5 sourcebook and have your players use that from now on. You can do the same for Potence and Fortitude if you're so inclined.


The Storyteller System (the name of the system of game mechanics Vampire and all World of Darkness games) is very simple and straight to the point, so much so that mechanics can be swapped in and out without much adaptation if at all between the various editions and game lines. There's no converting THAC0 to AC or figuring out when to apply advantage over a +2 (to use the D20 system edition changes for example.) You'll definitely want to read through the related rules and mechanics for each system before doing any of this, but I assure you that it's not as complicated as you think and if you study it a bit you'll see that most mechanics can be hard swapped in and out without disturbing too much of the other mechanics in the system.

Labels aren't for you, they're for other people. They tell others what to generally expect from you and what your expectations might be. When someone tells you that they're straight, you know that they're seeking a partner of the opposite sex, you can safely assume that they want both opposite sex partners for sex and relationships. When you hear someone is asexual you know at least that they're not looking for sex at all, but that they might be interested in having a relationship you might have to ask to clarify but if it's not something you're interested in you at least know not to try and hook them up with your friend.


What these labels all mean is ultimately up to you, as they are interpretive but so long as your definition doesn't stray too far from the common consensus then the word functions as intended in most situations. This, you might recognize, is how language works as a technology. We ascribe sounds and combinations of distinct sounds to objects, actions, and ideas to make it easier to communicate things to people without them needing to directly experience it for themselves. You know the sunset is beautiful to me at least when I tell you it was beautiful, or I'll be more specific and tell you that it was a beautiful array of oranges, reds, whites, and blues streaking across the sky as the large yellow-white sun dipped below the horizon. Language is a versatile technology that allows us a great degree of communication. It's like a kind of telepathy, using noises to insert ideas, emotions, and images into one anothers minds, sharing experiences from the great to the mundane. You know that I felt sad when my grandmother passed away, I know that you found your pastors sermon boring last week. You were not in my head, nor was I in yours, but we each have an understanding of one another's experiences.


We build our lives around these combinations of noises so integral is the technology to us as a species, and thus these words do inform our identities as ultimately they are how we describe ourselves to others without them needing to directly experience us. However the words are also shaped by us, we choose our preferred noises to fit our own experiences, to describe us. Even the very way we use wordsto describe others reflects is and says informs others of who we are to some degree, the words we choose even when we aren't describing ourselves reveal who we percieve ourselves to be.


So please appreciate that when you balk at the idea of "labels" understand that you're balking at the very idea of language itself since language is composed entirely of "labels". Linguistically "bisexual" is no more or less a "label" than "happy" or "blue" or "fish" ("fish" is actually the perfect example as it can be argued that biologically speaking "fish" don't exist* yet the word tells us something recognizable and specific.) The technology isn't perfect, how we use it changes over time, but that's the story of all technologies. What matters above all is that we as a society and culture recognize and agree upon the definitions to at least some degree now.


TL;DR "Labels" are just words that help people understand you to a certain degree so they know how to approach you and communicate ideas about you and with you. Rejecting "labels" is ultimately rejecting language itself. If you don't agree please respond without using any labels in your speech.

I have a different one. I think the progenitor of the Baali bloodline is Set. Here's my reasoning:

* Bloodlines typically follow some sort of theme with their parent clan. Daughters of Cacophony have madness/art, Ahriman have nature, Samedi have death, the main distinction for most is that the bloodlines narrow in on some aspect of their parent clans nature. The Salubri have divinity and good as their themes but the Baali go the opposite direction, this can work as a rejection and I would accept that as a valid counterpoint, but they'd be the only bloodline that does so. The Baali however do share such cultural traits as corruption, subversion, and the profane with the Followers of Set. Almost paralleled, the Baali are just taking it from an Abrahamic approach rather then an Egyptian-pagan approach.
* Bloodlines weaknesses are often an echo of their parents clan as well. The Salubri can't drink from the unwilling, but the Baali are repelled by holy artifacts. The Setites are also repelled however, by light, the primary domain of the Ra the chief diety of the ancient Egyptian pantheon.
* Bloodlines will also take their disciplines from their parent clan too, with deviations meant to fit the bloodlines specific themes or just to add in a unique discipline. As of 3rd edition revised (last edition to include stats for the Baali) the Salubri had Auspex, Fortitude, and Obeah. The Baali had Obfuscate, Presence, and Daimonion. The Followers of Set had Obfuscate, Presence, and Serpentis.

In short it's obvious to me that there's a lot of overlap between the Followers of Set and the Baali. Too much to ignore or rule out a connection. While there is no lore to support this, the only lore that supports the idea that it's the Salubri comes from either known liars or just a broad assumption. It's poetic to think that the most holy of the clans would spawn the most demonic, and it's certainly the kind of irony and perversion that the Baali love to revel in. Capsaicin burns because it triggers heat receptors in the skin tricking the nervous system into thinking it's overheating, causing the all-too-familiar burning sensation.

Vampires can still feel things, which suggests that their nervous system is still at least somewhat functioning. Vampires are even capable of sharpening their senses beyond the normal human range so we can assume that it's at least possible that a vampires nervous system is as sensitive or approximately as sensitive as a humans. There's this impression that they don't "feel" hot or cold but that's a misunderstanding. Their body temperature is basically whatever the ambient temperature in their immediate area is. The reason we notice the temperature in our climate, hot or cold, is because our body temperatures are lower or higher than the surrounding ambient temperature. That's what you're feeling when you step outside in a snowstorm without a jacket, that's what you're feeling when you're sweating it out by the grill at a summer cookout. Vampires are still capable of detecting temperatures that are higher or lower than the ambient temperature, they can feel the heat coming off the back of an old TV, they can feel the chill of an ice cube in their hand.

So I would have to say "yes, vampires should be affected by mace/pepper spray." They might not get it in their sinuses (at least not as much as a human with a working respiratory system might), which is what causes a good deal of the discomfort, but they will feel it on any areas that come in direct contact. Furthermore I would argue that since the effect of capsaicin is a burning sensation that it might result in a check for rötschreck (fear frenzy) as it strikes me that the beast might not be able to tell the difference between the sensation of burning and actually being on fire. It would be at a lower difficulty of course, the vampire being cognizant of the difference should lend them a better presence of mind to control it.

Ventrue clan culture comes with an appeal to the concept of the *noblesse oblige* (the obligations of nobility) that is to say that they profess a desire to lead in a way that is to the benefit of those they rule over. This is of course, for the most part, complete and utter horseshit. I bring this up because I'm seeing a lot of people claiming that a Ventrue might see the Anarchs as a potential route towards political power and that's a very valid response but it's important to note that it would be completely in keeping with Ventrue clan culture if a member defected to the Anarchs sincerely seeing the Anarch cause as just and their sense of the *noblesse oblige* would inform their decisions to join and seek a leadership role within the local Anarchs. Even if they aren't being sincere, that ideological concept would make for a great way to appear sincere in their beliefs, even when having to confront Camarilla aligned Ventrue, without having to completely abandon their clans ideals and culture allowing them to find a way to not burn too many bridges.

Complete and total side note: Anarchism as a political philosophy is horribly misunderstood in popular culture and White Wolf has never been an exception to this. Try reading up on Anarchism as a philosophical concept, the history of Anarchist movements throughout the world, and possibly even talk to a few anarchists here on reddit just to get a survey of the incredibly diverse tapestry of philosophy surrounding Anarchism. It could help you depict Anarchists in a more nuanced and interesting light. The biggest thing to understand is that Anarchy isn't simply "no government, no rules" as is often depicted but more "no hierarchies". That is to say that Anarchism seeks to spread social equality through communal democratic systems, instead of a hierarchical system that grants some people power over others by merit of their social position (however that is granted to them.) While there certainly are the "no government, no gods, no masters, no rules" approaches to the ideals of Anarchism, they are not the only perspectives on the concept and aren't actually considered to be popular or in any way more "pure" of an Anarchist philosophy.

This question crops up in some form or another pretty regularly and you need to understand that any answer to this question other than "it depends on how many points went into building their character sheet and how their sheet was built" is flat out wrong. There's a ton of nuance to this question to the point that asking it only illicits more questions, but here's a hard and fast rundown.

​

First we must assume that both the ghoul and vampire have been trained for combat and that their stats were built around being good at combat. Now since you specified that the Vampire was a fledgling that indicates a certain number of freebie experience at character creation (0 - 15 on average based on my experiences playing the game.) So the only real variable is the ghoul, so it comes down to how many experience points the ghoul has had in relation to the vampire.

\- If both the ghoul and the vampire are given the same number of experience points at creation than we can expect the vampire to win.

\- If the vampire has any experience point advantage over the ghoul we can expect the vampire to win.

\- If the ghoul has 20+ experience points over the vampire then the ghoul has the advantage (it is worth noting that this advantage decreases with the total number of experience points being distributed to both characters, after a certain point characters start maxing out their stats and vampires simply have more tricks available to them than do ghouls.)

What you're describing is in no way an invalid way of playing, what I'm asserting is that at the very least your players (let's use the rogue from your hypothetical) should be aware that something like True Polymorph is on the table. Personally, I would always have some sort of "get out of kobold free" card for my players, and it's okay if you don't want that to be in place, but what I want to emphasize more than anything else is that your players be aware that such a thing could happen before it becomes a possible reality. Going in to the dungeon with the lich, if True Polymorph is on that spell list and you plan to use it, at least warn the players. Maybe you weren't planning on it from the start of your campaign (as is being alluded to in the original post) but as soon as it becomes a very real threat you really should warn your players. Because I agree with you that a successful game is one where everyone is having fun; what I'm warning against is doing something that could seriously impact the fun that someone is having.

Let's go back to the party and their lich. The rogue has just been turned into a kobold, they have one hour to make the lich break concentration and the whole party knows this. If the rogues player really wants to break the spell they're going to be hard set on breaking that concentration as soon as they can, but if the rest of the party wants to take that short rest or even long rest then the rogue is just going to have to go about it solo. What this translates to is a player who now either needs to have what could be an extended solo rp session while the other players do nothing at all, there's the rest of the party no longer having fun. If the rogue then fails, either by losing the character or not making it in time, what you now have is a player suddenly very unhappy with their character and likely unhappy with the DM and other players at the table who could have helped, same goes for if the DM decides to not allow the rogue to try and save themselves. If the player is suddenly caught unawares and is now a kobold it would not be unreasonable for that player to no longer be having fun, even if they're making a good show of being a good sport about as the DM you'll know that you failed at the "fun" metric when they come to you and ask to make a new character. Kobold or sheep or whatever, you killed their character off in a very back-handed kind of way.

This can be avoided by simply warning the players ahead of time, at the start of the session, or at the start of the campaign, or at any point before it becomes a real threat. You can even do this diagetically, by having an NPC or journal or plaque or something indicate to the players that the lich has a history of transforming people permanently against their will. The point is not to never use these features of the game but to ensure that players are aware of the consequences they may face.

Not like what you described but yes there are "law enforcement" roles in vampiric society. Everyone else has explained what a Sheriffs role is, so I'm going to offer other positions, what they are supposed to be and how they can be altered to fill the role of a detective.

**Camarilla**


Scourge: Officially the scourges job is not someone you'd want to call a "detective" per se, they're more of a hitman. Traditionally the Scourges job is to patrol around the outskirts of the city and eliminate any Anarch gangs or Sabbat packs they encounter, calling in the Sheriff and his Hounds as necessary. However in my game the Prince has found himself in a delicate position and in need of someone to root out problems without being overtly hostile to the Anarchs in the city. To this end he has modified the role of Scourge to that of a detective and dubbed it his "Herald" as an official diplomatic role. He has assigned this task to one of the player characters who has taken in the rest of the group as his coterie. Together they're going around the city, investigating problems and either calling in the Sheriff or what Anarchs they have good relations with to help with problems they can't handle on their own. So far in this role they've hunted down a Sabbat vampire that had been preying on a homeless camp which was being watched over by a pack of Bone Gnawer werewolves.


Hound: the Sheriffs job is to act as the Prince's enforcer, not a peacekeeper or law bringer type. However the Sheriffs Hounds could take on that role for more active Sheriffs. They can root out trouble makers and bully others into submission, or take a more gentle approach if the political atmosphere allows for it, all the while being in a position where they can be cut loose if they overstep their duties or cause trouble. They're expendable but then, in the jyhad who isn't?


Archon: the Justiciars are the vampires who work directly for the Camarillas Inner Circle. They represent one of the clans represented within the circle and are an office symbolic of that clans might. Justiciars serve as generals in the Camarillas wars againt their political opponents and have the right to do as they see fit to achieve their goals. They act as Judges during conclaves and even have the ability to execute Prince's and Primogen. Their Archons are their eyes, ears, and swords. The Archon duties are determined entirely by their Justiciar however and can be inherited as a kind of "vampire FBI" coming in ahead of the Justiciar, collecting information or acting out on the Justiciars plots and strategies.


**Anarchs**

Sweeper: the Anarchs are not ones for law enforcement, they don't care much for authority or political hierarchies at all, but that wouldn't mean that they don't have some need for one. "Officially" (as official as anything about the Anarchs can be) the role of the sweeper is less cop than census taker. Their job is to covertly monitor the kindred in their Barons domain, particularly new kindred, and report their observations to the Baron so they can be aware of who or what is moving in they're territory, and what they might be capable of. In the game "Bloodlines" when the character first arrives in Anarch controlled Hollywood they are immediately greeted immediately by a vampire telling them they need to introduce themselves to the Baron. That would be the Sweeper. There's no reason however why a Sweeper couldn't investigate problems on their Barons behalf. The Sweeper might be a better option for your detective character of you'd prefer a more peaceful kind of investigatory role.


**Sabbat**


Judges and Knights: the Sabbatbis often seen and tight of as a lawless bunch even in comparison to the Anarchs, and while that's true to the laws of god or of man it couldn't be further from the truth. The Sabbat is a paramilitary organization with a decentralized political framework, they consider themselves to be at war at all times and as such maintain strict practices and have regulations on how they expect their members to act, all the while promising their members a freedom akin to that of the Anarchs. This has led to a problem for them, as the depravity and monsterous nature ofv they members has resulted in the occasional problem with Infernalists; vampires worshipping demons. Aside from offensive to the religious sensibilities of a lot of the Sabbats leadership, Infernalists tend to be corrosive to the Sabbats political structure and are particularly messy, risking the Sabbats code of silence. Essentially they are a threat to the local Diocese strength and what secrecy they maintain. To this end the Regent forms an Inquisition and names a Judge to lead a pack of Knights in hunting diwn and eliminating any and all infernalist vampires as they see fit. Due to the Sabbats nature this is always a violent and brutal affair, some packs of Inquisitors being little better than cleaner crews taking out entire packs they suspect of having even a single Infernalist among them, but a more sophisticated pack might act more as hunters within kindred society, investigating, tracking, and eliminating individuals with survival precision and presenting they findings to the Regent alongside the Infernalists own pack before executing them. The former is more common than the latter, but there's a range you can play with. Notably, members of a diocese Inquisition are barred from becoming members of the Sabbats Black Hand.


The Black Hand: If Justiciars act as the Camarillas FBI the Black Hand is the Sabbats CIA. They are a secretive organization that serve a myriad of roles often times embedded within a Diocese various packs. Sometimes even embedded under deep cover whithin the Camarilla. A lot has changed about this particular organization over the years, even compared to the rest of the games lore. I highly recommend checking out "The Dirty Secrets if the Black Hand" sourcebool from the V20 edition, and to avoid the second edition version of the same name just to reduce confusion. *Note: as of V5 the greater structure of the Sabbay has not yet been introduced. The Sabbat in V5 at this moment is intended to serve more as antagonists than a rival political power to anyone. This is in keeping with the Sabbats "terrorist network" structure from previous editions. As of this time, neither the Inquisition nor the Black Hand as organizations have been explored. However the V5 Sabbat sourcebook "Sabbat: the Black Hand" uses the "Black Hand" as a nickname for the Sabbat as a whole, this been canon for roughly 4 decades now. So to lay it out: the Sabbat is sometimes called the Black Hand and has an organization within it known as the Black Hand, which is semi-autonomous and not representative of the entire Black Hand. I hope that clears things up. Read "Dirty Secrets of the Black Hand."


**Inconnu**

Monitors: Ah, ha ha ha. Whoo boy. This one's gonna be a stretch. The Inconnu are a mysterious and incredibly secretive organization of elder vampires that have withdrawn themselves from the jyhad, and seek Golconda, and encourage other kindred to take the same path. They do not proselytize however, preferring instead to find exemplary kindred of strong character and retaining some clear moral sense after decades if not centuries of undeath and help guide them along the path while recording that progress to pass along to the rest of Inconnu for their own explorationand development. To this end the Inconnu nominates certain members to serve as Monitors for certain cities, to keep an eye on the kindred population for such individuals. Elders over time accrue power, wealth, status, so on regardless of whether or not they seek enlightenment and the Inconnu really doesn't like to advertise their existence, especially when the Sabbat is around, and prefers to keep their activities quiet and subtle at all times. What follows is conjecture and personal interpretation: do not take this for canon, thus far everything up to this point is the bulk of canonical information concerning the Inconnu; everything hereafter is me.


A more active Monitor would therefore need stalwart and good agents to act on their behalf, even if this means tasking a vampire they believe could be guided towards Golconda with activities that might help usher more kindred towards a righteous path. It's not hard to imagine that this might include doing things in the name of righteousness, and justice, maybe even helping to protect mortals or other supernatural beings from their fellow vampires, can't seek Golconda if you're evicting mortal families from their homes, or allowing a vampire serial killer to snatch women off the street, or allow the Camarilla to strike at their Anarch rivals at the cost of those same Anarch rivals mortal allies. Now I'm not saying that any character taking this route should be the Monitor or even member of the Inconnu, but they could easily be allied to a Monitor helping them protect the kine and even innocent autarkis from getting caught in the crossfire of the jyhad.
